content: Transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTNB) is a respiratory condition that occurs in newborns shortly after birth. It is characterized by an abnormally rapid breathing rate, exceeding the normal range of 40 to 60 breaths per minute for newborns. This condition is thought to result from retained fetal lung fluid and is more commonly observed in infants born at or beyond 35 weeks of gestation, particularly those delivered via cesarean section without labor. TTNB typically resolves within 24 to 48 hours. Management is primarily supportive and may involve the administration of supplemental oxygen and, in some cases, antibiotics. The pathophysiology of TTNB is believed to involve several mechanisms. First, the higher incidence of TTNB in infants delivered by cesarean section suggests that the condition may result from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid through the pulmonary lymphatic system. This retained fluid increases airway resistance and decreases lung compliance. Second, pulmonary immaturity has been implicated as a contributing factor. For instance, some affected newborns have been found to lack phosphatidylglycerol, a marker of lung maturity. Third, a mild deficiency in surfactant, a substance critical for reducing surface tension in the lungs, has also been proposed as a potential cause. The diagnosis of TTNB often involves imaging studies, particularly chest X-rays. Findings on chest X-rays may include evidence of pulmonary edema, such as airspace opacities, prominent interstitial markings, indistinct pulmonary vasculature, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly. The lung volumes in these infants may appear normal or increased.
